etymology: Latin immediatus — without a middle. The AV uses it for action with no delay: nets dropped, fever gone, scales fallen, throne seen.
biblical_def: Immediately is time without an intervening excuse. They immediately left the ship and their father, and followed Him (Mat 4:22). He lifted her, and immediately the fever left her (Mar 1:31). Scales fell, and immediately he received sight and was baptized (Act 9:18). John was immediately in the Spirit before the throne (Rev 4:2). The word rebukes delayed obedience dressed as process. Mark loves it because the King's word does not wait for a committee. Modern spirituality praises slow journeys as wisdom. Sometimes slowness is unbelief. When Christ calls, nets drop now. When He speaks clean, uncleanness leaves now. Delay is not automatically discernment. Immediately is the adverb of authority meeting a will that yields. The middle that would stand between command and deed is refused. That is not impulsiveness. It is the right speed of a creature under a speaking Lord.

etymology: Middle English in stede — in the place of. The AV's substitution word: rib for flesh, Levites for firstborn, crown for Vashti, fir for thorn.
biblical_def: Instead names a replacement in a real place, not a mood swap. The LORD took a rib and closed up the flesh instead thereof (Gen 2:21). Israel gathered stubble instead of straw (Exo 5:12). Judgment trades sweet smell for stink, beauty for burning (Isa 3:24). Thistles grow instead of wheat when a man will not repent (Job 31:40). The Levites are taken instead of all the firstborn (Num 3:12). Esther is made queen instead of Vashti (Est 2:17). Instead of the thorn, the fir; instead of the brier, the myrtle (Isa 55:13). The gospel's great instead is substitution: He who knew no sin made sin for us. Modern talk of instead is lifestyle preference. Scripture's instead is place-taking: office, judgment, mercy, and atonement occupy a slot something else held. Do not flatten it into rebranding. A rib instead of an open side is surgery. A Substitute instead of the sinner is salvation.

etymology: Old English ordinal of twenty. The AV uses it to date cloud, feast, word, and siege — history with a numbered day, not a vibe.
biblical_def: Twentieth is the ordinal that pins a holy history to a calendar. On the twentieth day of the second month, the second year, the cloud was taken up from the tabernacle of the testimony (Num 10:11). Unleavened bread runs until the one and twentieth day at even (Exo 12:18). In the one and twentieth day of the seventh month the word of the LORD came by Haggai (Hag 2:1). Ezekiel dates a word to the seven and twentieth year (Eze 29:17). God numbers days. Israel marches when the cloud lifts on a dated morning. Feasts have a last even. Prophets speak on a numbered day, not when inspiration feels ripe. Modern spirituality is allergic to calendars except for branding launches. The wilderness clock is a rebuke. To despise ordinals is to despise the God who acts in time. The twentieth is as theological as any feast day: a numbered morning when the cloud moved and the camp had to follow.

etymology: Old English understandan — to stand under a meaning. AV past of understand: books, sanctuary, opened Scripture — not a vibe of being seen.
biblical_def: Understood is the past of standing under a word until it yields sense. The people made great mirth because they had understood the words that were declared unto them (Neh 8:12). Asaph did not understand the wicked's prosperity until he went into the sanctuary; then understood I their end (Psa 73:17). Daniel understood by books the seventy years of Jerusalem's desolations (Dan 9:2). The risen Lord opened their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures (Luk 24:45). The word is not empathy as the age uses it. It is comprehension of declared words, prophetic books, and the end of the wicked. Therapy asks to be understood. Ezra's people understood the law and then ate, drank, and sent portions. Sanctuary, not self-talk, teaches the end of the prosperous wicked. Opened Scripture is Christ's gift; closed ears are not a learning style.

etymology: Latin reicere — to throw back. AV past of refuse-and-cast: Israel rejecting the LORD's reign; men rejecting the Servant and the Son of man.
biblical_def: Rejected is the recorded cast-off. They have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them (1Sa 8:7). He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows (Isa 53:3). The Son of man must be rejected of the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and rise (Mar 8:31). Coming to the living stone, disallowed of men, but chosen of God (1Pe 2:4). The word is not a self-esteem wound. It is treason against reign, and the appointed path of the Servant. Israel rejected kingship's true King when they demanded Saul. Men rejected the Man of sorrows. Courts rejected Christ unto death. God chose what men disallowed. Do not baptize every social slight as this verb. The canon's rejected is about reign, atonement, and the stone. Therapeutic talk of rejection as inner injury steals the word from 1 Samuel 8 and Isaiah 53.

etymology: Latin quaestio — a seeking, an inquiry. In the AV: Christ's counter-question, silenced opponents, the Jerusalem dispute, and conscience at the shambles.
biblical_def: A question is an inquiry that seeks a binding answer, not a pose. Jesus will ask one question about authority before He answers theirs (Mar 11:29). After a discreet answer, no man durst ask Him any question (Mar 12:34). Paul and Barnabas go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question (Act 15:2). Eat what is sold, asking no question for conscience sake (1Co 10:25). The age treats question as a virtue in itself — always interrogate, never submit. Scripture treats some questions as traps, some as church cases, and some as needless scruples. Christ's question exposes. The council's question is settled by apostles and elders, not by endless thread. Shambles-questions can become a law against liberty. Do not baptize skepticism as holiness. A good question wants the truth that binds. A bad question wants to keep the King from answering.

etymology: Latin necessitas — that which must be. AV range: saints' want, apostolic woe if the gospel is not preached, cheerful gift versus compulsion, death of a testator.
biblical_def: Necessity is what must be, or the want that must be met. Distributing to the necessity of saints (Rom 12:13). Necessity is laid upon me; woe if I preach not the gospel (1Co 9:16). Give not grudgingly, or of necessity: God loveth a cheerful giver (2Co 9:7). The Philippians sent once and again unto Paul's necessity (Php 4:16). Where a testament is, there must also of necessity be the death of the testator (Heb 9:16). The word is not fate as pagans mean it. It is constraint under office, want under charity, and legal must under covenant. Therapeutic talk of my needs steals the noun. Saints have necessity; apostles have a laid-on woe; givers must not be compelled as if tax; a will requires a death. Do not flatten those into self-care. Gospel necessity is a chain on the preacher, not a coupon for the self.

etymology: English other + wise — in another manner. The AV uses it for the fork: alms seen of men, passover not as written, grace versus works, a mind God will correct.
biblical_def: Otherwise is the other manner that forfeits a reward, breaks a rule, or exposes a contradiction. Alms before men to be seen: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father (Mat 6:1). Many ate the passover otherwise than it was written; Hezekiah prayed for pardon (2Ch 30:18). If by grace, then no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace (Rom 11:6). If ye be otherwise minded, God shall reveal even this unto you (Php 3:15). The word is a fork in the road, not a soft synonym for alternatively as catalogs use it. Secret alms or no Father-reward. Written passover or pardon begged. Grace or works — mix them and you have neither. A wrong mind is not a valid option; it is something God may yet reveal away. Do not hear otherwise as infinite choice. Hear it as the other path that empties grace, reward, or ordinance.
